extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of satirical/comic literature (e.g., Rabelais scholars, humorists)
extracted.subtask_description: Producing or analyzing satirical, grotesque comic prose in the Rabelaisian/renaissance tradition — broad scenic narration, dialogue-driven episodes, and episodic practical jokes. Emphasizes parody, bodily/scatalogical humor, and absurd invention of customs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor brevity over rambling
rubrics_metrics.description: "I hate a gibble-gabble and a rimble-ramble talk. I am for a man of brevity.", "There is too long a lecture by half".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use short, punchy lines and cut long-winded lectures; value concise, pithy remarks as a comic virtue. The text explicitly contrasts entertaining brevity with tedious 'gibble-gabble' and 'rimble-ramble' lectures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use practical trickery/pranks as plot engine
rubrics_metrics.description: Panurge throws a ram overboard causing the whole flock and their keepers to follow and be drowned; Panurge arranges the drowning/removal of Dingdong and his sheep.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make mischief and cunning schemes central to episode progression: set up a plausible exploit, execute a trick that produces escalating absurd consequences, and let the narrator or protagonist gloat over the 'sport' gained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amplify comedy through absurd/excessive lists and inventories
rubrics_metrics.description: Long catalogues of animal parts and their ludicrous uses: "the inward members, the shoulders, the legs, the knuckles, the neck, the breast, the liver, the spleen, the tripes, the kidneys, the bladder..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy exhaustive, hyper-detailed lists that attribute ridiculous functions to mundane items; the piling up of detail itself produces comic effect and mock-scientific authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grotesque and scatological bodily/food humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent references to urine, dung, pills made from dung, 'a turd on’t', 'a fart for the money', extravagant eating/feeding images (hogs on myrobolans, sows fed with orange-flowers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not shy from bodily/food-related imagery; bodily functions and culinary excess are used to shock, parody refinement, and produce gross-but-funny juxtaposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invent incongruous customs and marriages to satirize society
rubrics_metrics.description: Islands where kinship terms are absurd (people call each other 'my butter'/'my eggs'); weddings like marrying a pear to a cheese or a boot to a buskin are described as normal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create fictional social conventions that are internally coherent but wildly different from readers' expectations; use these invented customs to lampoon real social institutions (marriage, kinship, status).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody learned/authoritative language and pseudo-scholarship
rubrics_metrics.description: Speakers invoke Aristotle, Galen, and legal/clerical forms then apply them absurdly (e.g., 'as Aristotle, lib. 9. De. Hist. Animal., mark them for the most silly and foolish animals', the seller's canting and learned-sounding claims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mimic academic, legal, or clerical registers and cite authorities mock-seriously, then subvert them by applying to trivial or absurd matters; macaronic Latin adds comic faux-erudition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use role inversion and burlesque of social ranks
rubrics_metrics.description: Monks delighting in kitchens, nobles kissed pages disguised as women, servants staged to thrash a catchpole under the pretense of a wedding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flip expected social roles (clerics in kitchens, pages as women, servants performing ceremonies) to create comic tension and critique social pretensions; stage burlesque scenes where formality collapses into farce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody institutional/ceremonial forms (legal, matrimonial, religious)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mock-ceremonies: the 'form of matrimony must be read' to cover up a trouncing of a catchpole; use of 'Legem pone', 'Matter of breviary'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repurpose solemn rituals (marriage rites, legal summonses, liturgical phrases) for profane or comic ends to expose hypocrisy and create irony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rapid repartee and dialogic short exchanges for comedic timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent short back-and-forths: 'Patience, said Panurge'; 'A murrain seize thee...'; 'A fart for the money, said Panurge'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure scenes as quick exchanges with interruptions, retorts, and tag lines; brisk dialogue sustains momentum and delivers punchlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ onomatopoeia, gibberish, and comic noises
rubrics_metrics.description: Strings like 'rr, rrr, rrrr, rrrrr, hoh Robin, rr, rrrrrrr', 'baea, baea, baea', 'Hho, hho, hho... brrou, rrou...' appear as sound effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert vocal noises, gibberish, and animal cries to heighten physical comedy and produce carnivalesque atmosphere; such sounds break language expectations and add visceral humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration and hyperbole to create ludicrous claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Seller's claims: sheep descended from the ram that wafted Phryxus and Helle; 'above three hundred thousand, all relations' could march out; horns that will grow asparagus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make outrageous, untestable claims and escalate them — tall tales and hyperbole create disbelief and ridicule targets (merchants, charlatans, social myths).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mix languages and registers (macaronic verse) for comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Macaronic lines and interjections mix Latin, French, and rustic speech ('Beati immaculati in via. Matter of breviary', macaronic verse quoted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blend languages, scholarly Latin and colloquial speech to create register clash; macaronic verse and code-switching mock pretension and produce comic dissonance.
